To mummify means to preserve a dead body by drying it out so completely that it stops decaying (rotting) and stays intact — sometimes for thousands of years.

The result of mummification is called a mummy — a dried, preserved dead body.

When a living thing dies, its body normally starts to break down. Bacteria, moisture, and air all work together to decompose (rot) the body until nothing is left but bones or dust. This is the natural process.

Mummification stops that process. It works by removing almost all moisture from the body. Bacteria and decay need moisture to do their work. Take away the moisture, and the body essentially "freezes in time" — not by cold, but by dryness.

Think of it like this: a fresh grape rots within days. But a raisin — which is just a grape with all its moisture removed — lasts for a very long time. Mummifying a body works on the same basic principle.

Mummify can be used in two ways:

1. When someone does it deliberately (to something):
This is called the transitive use — there is a person or group performing the action on a body.

"The ancient Egyptians used to mummify their pharaohs after death."
"The priests carefully mummified the body using salt and linen bandages."

Here, a human agent is intentionally preserving a body through a process.

2. When it happens on its own (naturally):
This is called the intransitive use — no one is doing it on purpose; conditions simply cause it to happen.

"The body mummified naturally after being buried in the dry desert sand."
"The cold, airless cave caused the remains to slowly mummify over centuries."

The most famous example comes from ancient Egypt, where mummification was a deeply religious and cultural practice. The Egyptians believed the body needed to be preserved so the soul could return to it in the afterlife.

The process involved steps like:

  • Removing internal organs (such as the brain, lungs, and intestines) since these decay the fastest
  • Drying the body using a special salt called natron, which absorbed all moisture
  • Wrapping the body tightly in linen bandages
  • Placing the mummy in a decorated coffin or tomb

Other ancient civilizations — such as the Incas in South America and certain cultures in Asia — also deliberately mummified their dead, though their methods differed.

When we say they mummified the body, we mean they carried out this entire deliberate process of preservation.

Mummification doesn't always require human effort. Nature can mummify a body on its own if the conditions are right. The key ingredient is always the same: something that stops moisture and decay.

Common natural conditions that mummify a body:

  • Extreme dry heat — like a desert. The hot, dry air pulls all moisture out of the body rapidly before decay can take hold.
  • Extreme cold — like glaciers or permafrost (permanently frozen ground). The freezing temperature preserves the body almost perfectly. "Ötzi the Iceman," a 5,300-year-old body discovered in the Alps, was naturally mummified by ice.
  • Highly salty environments — Salt draws out moisture, the same way it preserves food.
  • Peat bogs — Waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen swamps can preserve bodies in a unique way, though this is slightly different from typical mummification; these are often called "bog bodies."

In all these cases, you can say the body was mummified by the environment.

Like many words, mummify can also be used in a figurative sense — meaning you use it to describe something that isn't literally a dead body, but shares the quality of being dried out, rigid, lifeless, or frozen in time without changing or evolving.

"The organization had mummified over the decades — it refused to change with the times."

(Meaning: it had become stiff, rigid, and dead in spirit, like a mummy.)

"He sat in that chair so still and pale, he looked absolutely mummified."

(Meaning: he resembled a mummy — motionless, dried out in appearance.)

This figurative usage is less common than the literal one, but you will encounter it in literature and everyday speech.
All the Forms of the Word

Since you'll see this word in different forms, here's how it changes:

FormExample
mummify"They decided to mummify the king."
mummifies"The dry air mummifies anything buried in it."
mummified"The mummified body was discovered in the tomb."
mummifying"The salt was slowly mummifying the tissue."
mummification (noun)"The mummification process took 70 days."
mummy (noun — the result)"The archaeologists unwrapped the mummy."

To mummify = to preserve a dead body (by natural conditions or deliberate human action) through drying it out so completely that it does not rot, keeping it intact for a very long time.

If you ever see the word mummify or mummified, ask yourself: Is something being preserved by having its moisture taken away, preventing decay? If yes — that's exactly what the word means.
